1:
Gill begins with the rendering. Instances of the serpent's subtlety are many — the head hidden when struck at, the ear stopped at the charmer's voice — but by these it does not appear more subtle than any other creature; the fox greatly exceeds it. The words may therefore be read "that serpent," the particular one spoken of afterwards, or "the serpent was become," made more subtle not naturally but through Satan being in it and using it to gain his point. A real serpent is meant, as the curse afterwards pronounced upon it shows, yet not that only, but as possessed and used. Ellicott looks rather to the wordplay. The contrast would be plainer rendered "now they were both naked (arumim) ... but the serpent was subtil (arum)". The quality was in itself innocent and even admirable, the Septuagint translating it prudent; the tempter merely made use of it, and she would not be surprised at being addressed by so sagacious a creature. Clarke calls this the most difficult and most important narrative in the whole book of God, and refuses the received word: nachash carries three distinct senses in Scripture, and he traces the root to an Arabic verb meaning he departed, drew off, lay hid, seduced, which yields both the name of a creature of the ape kind and a name of the Devil.

Behind the creature the expositors put one name. Henry holds it certain that the devil beguiled Eve — by creation an angel of light, by sin an apostate and a rebel. This that attacked our first parents was surely the prince of the devils: no sooner a sinner than a Satan, no sooner a traitor than a tempter. He knew he could not destroy man but by debauching him; the whole race had here, as it were, but one neck, and at that Satan struck. Whether it was only the appearance of a serpent or a real one actuated and possessed by the devil he leaves open; by God's permission it might be either. Calvin comes at the difficulty from the other side: the innate subtlety of the serpent did not prevent Satan from making use of the animal, for requiring an instrument he chose the one most suitable; and hitherto having held no communication with men, he clothed himself with the person of an animal, under which he might open for himself the way of access. Wesley adds what made the approach unremarkable to her: it is not improbable that reason and speech were then the known properties of the serpent, and therefore Eve was not surprised at his reasoning and speaking.

Keil and Delitzsch set the approach against what man already had: food in the fruit of the trees, a field of labour in the care of the garden, a region for his intellect in the animal and vegetable kingdom, a positive law in the tree of knowledge, and in the woman a suitable companion — and it was out of the midst of that animal world that the tempter came. Calvin asks why Moses keeps back the name of Satan, and answers that the Spirit then purposely used obscure figures, clear light being reserved for the kingdom of Christ; the prophets show they understood him. Ellicott hears surprise in the opening question, as if the tempter could not bring himself to believe such a command had been given. Neither the serpent nor the woman uses the title Jehovah-Elohim common throughout this section: it is the impersonal God of creation the tempter names, and she follows his lead, forgetting that it was Jehovah, the personal Being in covenant with them, who had given the command. Since the leading point is that the temptation came from without and through the woman, Ellicott holds the curious questions better left unanswered.
2:
Gill reads the woman's reply charitably. She answered him that spoke in the serpent, whom she might well take for a messenger from heaven, a holy angel; had she known who it was she might be chargeable with imprudence in carrying on the conversation at all, yet even so her answer may have had a good design — partly to set the matter in a true light, partly to set forth the goodness and liberality of God in the large provision he had made and the generous grant he had given them. From this discourse, Gill adds, Plato no doubt had his notion of the first men discoursing with beasts. Of the tree itself he observes that she gives it no name, which perhaps had not yet been given; its name in the preceding chapter is written by anticipation, and most likely it took that name from the event. Clarke fastens on the clause she does add. Did not the woman add "neither shall ye touch it" to what God had before spoken? Some of the Jewish writers, serious only on comparative trifles, say that as soon as she asserted it the serpent pushed her against the tree: see, thou hast touched it, and art still alive.

At the flat denial Calvin marks a change of tactics. Satan now springs more boldly forward, and because he sees a breach open before him he breaks through in a direct assault; he is never wont to engage in open war until we voluntarily expose ourselves to him, naked and unarmed. He approaches at first with blandishments, but once he has stolen in he dares to exalt himself petulantly and with proud confidence against God — seizing on the woman's doubt, he penetrates further, to turn it into a direct negative. He no longer asks doubtingly whether the command be true, but openly accuses God of falsehood. Fatal temptation, when God is threatening us with death and we not only securely sleep but hold God himself in derision. Clarke says the same more shortly: here the father of lies at once appears, and appears in flatly contradicting the assertion of God, insinuating the impossibility of her dying, as though she had been created immortal. Gill takes up the ground offered for it. God foreknows the consequence, that eating would issue not in death but in a clearer understanding, and is unwilling they should enjoy it — the insinuation being that God hates the creatures he has made, and will not have them as happy as they might be.

On the promise itself the translators divide. Clarke holds that kelohim should be rendered like God, the Syriac alone of the versions having hit the true meaning; the object was to persuade them they should become wise and powerful as God, knowledge being power, and able to exist for ever independently of him. Ellicott renders it the same way and narrows it: as Elohim himself, in the particular quality of knowing good and evil. It was a high bait, and Eve, who had at first answered rightly, dallied with it and was lost — though we must not comment too severely, for it was no mean desire that led her astray. She longed for more knowledge and greater perfection, but the means were in violation of the command. As usual the tempter kept his promise to the ear: she knew good and evil, but only by feeling evil within herself, so that it was by moral degradation and not by intellectual insight that the wish was fulfilled. Calvin puts the diagnosis in one line. Eve erred in not regulating the measure of her knowledge by the will of God, and we all suffer daily under the same disease, whereas the principal point of wisdom is a well-regulated sobriety in obedience.
6:
Gill puts us at the tree with her. Being near it, and perhaps just at it when the serpent first attacked her, she looked the more wishfully and could discern nothing in the fruit that showed it bad or unfit to be eaten, or why it should be forbidden; on the contrary it had a most promising aspect, as delicious and salutary as any other in the garden. Henry says the same of her judgment. It was said of all the rest of the fruit-trees that they were pleasant to the sight and good for food, and in her eye this was like all the rest; and when there is thought to be no more harm in forbidden fruit than in other fruit, sin lies at the door. Or it may have been coveted the more because prohibited — nitimur in vetitum, we desire what is forbidden. Clarke counts the inducements and finds them familiar. The fruit appeared wholesome; its beauty whetted appetite; the promise of wisdom was a further motive. From these three sources all natural and moral evil sprang, and they are exactly what the apostle calls the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye, and the pride of life.

Henry then counts the steps, not steps upward but downward. She saw: a great deal of sin comes in at the eyes, and at those windows Satan throws in the fiery darts that pierce the heart. She took: it was her own act and deed, for the devil did not put it into her mouth; Satan may tempt but he cannot force. She did eat: perhaps she did not intend, when she looked, to take, nor when she took to eat, but this was the result — the way of sin is downhill, and a man cannot stop himself when he will. She gave also to her husband: those that have themselves done ill are commonly willing to draw in others, and as was the devil, so was Eve, no sooner a sinner than a tempter. Wesley weighs what Adam's eating implied: unbelief of God's word and confidence in the devil's, discontent with his present state, and ambition of the honour that comes not from God; he would be both his own carver and his own master, and his sin was in one word disobedience. Ellicott finds his whole demeanour extraordinary. It is the woman who is tempted, and she has not to seek him, for he shares the gathered fruit with her at once; his passive behaviour is as striking as her eagerness.

Calvin traces the fault further back than the hand that reached out. This impure look, infected with the poison of concupiscence, was both the messenger and the witness of an impure heart: she could previously behold the tree with such sincerity that no desire to eat of it affected her mind, for the faith she had in the word of God was the best guardian of her heart and of all her senses; she had passed by it a hundred times with an unmoved and tranquil look. What then was the sin? The opinion of some of the ancients, that they were allured by intemperance of appetite, he calls puerile — where there was such abundance of the choicest fruits, what daintiness could there be about one kind? Augustine is more correct, that pride was the beginning of all evils. But fuller still: the woman was first led away from the word of God through unbelief, so unbelief was the root of defection, just as faith alone unites us to God; unbelief opened the door to ambition, and ambition proved the parent of rebellion. Ellicott states the same want positively — the resistance she failed to offer would have been possible only by a living faith in the spoken word of God.
7:
Gill insists the opening was of the mind, not the body, and that what it showed was disagreeable and distressing rather than the advance promised: their eyes were opened to see that they had been deceived, that they had broken the commandment and incurred the displeasure of their benefactor, and to see what blessings they had lost — communion with God, the dominion of the creatures — and what misery they had involved their posterity in. Ellicott dates the consciousness of guilt to the moment of eating, and argues from it that they ate together; otherwise Eve would have led Adam into sin after her own understanding had been enlightened to perceive the consequences. Their increased knowledge brought only shame: their minds were awakened and enlarged, but the price they paid was their innocence and peace. Clarke measures the loss by what Adam had been. A short time before he could name all the creatures according to their natures; now he does not know the first principle concerning the divine nature, that it is omnipresent, and so tries to hide among the trees. Their judgment was confused too: it was shameful to break the commandment, and no shame at all to go naked where clothing was not needed.

On the covering itself the questions are botanical and moral together. Keil and Delitzsch name what was lost as that blessed blindness, the ignorance of innocence, which knows nothing of nakedness; the discovery excited shame, which they sought to conceal by an outward covering. The word always denotes the fig-tree, not the pisang, whose leaves are twelve feet long — there would have been no necessity to sew those together at all; and what was made were aprons worn round the hips. Ellicott agrees against the pisang and fastens instead on the verb sewed. The Syriac translator, feeling the difficulty of supposing Eve acquainted with needlework, renders it that they stuck leaves together, but the word implies something more elaborate; probably some time elapsed between the sin and its punishment, allowing not merely a first hasty covering but something more careful, and the word rendered aprons is more correctly girdles. Calvin asks what the girdles were for, and answers that they were to keep God at a distance as by an invincible barrier. There is none of us who does not smile at their folly, since it was ridiculous to place such a covering before the eyes of God; and yet we are all infected with the same disease, resorting to vain trifles as if it were an easy thing to delude him.

The hour of the visit is itself part of the reproach. Clarke thinks God used to converse with them in the garden at the decline of the day, in the evening breeze, and that this was probably the time our first parents employed in the more solemn acts of worship: the time for that worship is come again, and God is in his place, but they are hidden among the trees. Ellicott reads the verb as reflexive, walking for pleasure, so that Jehovah appears as the owner of the garden taking His daily exercise; the primary lesson is that hitherto man had lived in close communication with God. He then traces the two flights: the first result of sin was shame, which man tried to cure by covering his person, and the second was fear, which he would cure by departing still farther from God. Calvin sees the covering fail at once. All bury the disgrace of their vices under flimsy leaves until God by his voice strikes inwardly upon their consciences; and he who had found a few leaves unavailing now fled to whole trees, as we are accustomed, when shut out from frivolous cavils, to frame new excuses that may hide us under a denser shade.
9:
Henry treats the question as the opening of a trial — the arraignment of these deserters before the righteous Judge of heaven and earth, who, though not tied to observe formalities, proceeds with all possible fairness that he may be justified when he speaks. Not as if God did not know where he was; thus he would enter the process against him. Some make it a bemoaning question, poor Adam, what has become of thee; Henry takes it rather as upbraiding, and in order to conviction — not in what place, but in what condition. Is this all thou hast gotten by eating forbidden fruit? Those who by sin have gone astray should seriously consider where they are: afar off from all good, in the midst of their enemies, in bondage to Satan, and in the high road to utter ruin. Wesley reads the same enquiry as mercy, a gracious pursuit in order to his recovery; had God not called to him, his condition had been as desperate as that of fallen angels. Gill notes only who is speaking. The Jerusalem Targum has here the Word of the Lord God, the second Person, and this, he says, is the voice Adam is said to have heard before.

Calvin asks why a second call was needed, since they had already been smitten by the voice of God and lay confounded under the trees. The former was a confused sound which had no sufficient force to press upon the conscience; God now approaches nearer, and from the tangled thicket of trees draws him, however unwilling and resisting, forth into the midst. In the same manner we are alarmed as soon as his law sounds in our ears, but presently snatch at shadows, until he, calling more vehemently, compels us to come forward, arraigned at his tribunal. Paul calls this the life of the law, when it slays us by charging us with our sins; for as long as we are pleased with ourselves and inflated with a false notion that we are alive, the law is dead to us, because we blunt its point by our hardness. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point about the purpose of the question: the man could not hide himself from God, who asked not because he was ignorant of the hiding-place, but to bring him to a confession of his sin. And when Adam answered that he had hidden through fear of his nakedness, he sought to hide the sin behind its consequences, his disobedience behind the feeling of shame.

The answer, all three agree, stops short of confession. Henry observes that Adam does not own his guilt, and yet in effect confesses it by owning his shame and fear; it is the common fault and folly of those that have done an ill thing, when questioned about it, to acknowledge no more than what is so manifest that they cannot deny it. He was afraid because he was naked — not only unarmed, and therefore afraid to contend with God, but unclothed, and therefore afraid so much as to appear before him. Calvin presses harder: Adam imputes his fear to the voice of God and to his own nakedness, as if he had never before heard God speak without being alarmed, or been sweetly exhilarated by his speech. His excessive stupidity appears in this, that he fails to recognise the cause of shame in his sin, and so shows he does not yet feel his punishment enough to confess his fault; notwithstanding his fig-leaves, he still dreads the presence of God. Clarke sets down the two immediate consequences of the fall — shame, at the ingratitude of the rebellion, and fear, at finding themselves deceived and exposed to the death they had been promised exemption from — and remarks that they have invariably been its fruits ever since.
11:
Henry marks the point of the first question. Though God knows all our sins, he will know them from us, and requires an ingenuous confession of them — not that he may be informed, but that we may be humbled; and in the examination he reminds Adam of the command he had given, I thy Maker, I thy Master, I thy benefactor. Sin appears most plain and most sinful in the glass of the commandment, therefore God sets it before him, and in it we should see our faces. Ellicott sees the same question turning him from the symptom to the disease. Adam had given as his excuse what was really the consequence of his sin, and by asking who told him he was naked God awakens his conscience and makes him feel that what he had described as a want was the result of his own act; as long as a man feels sorrow only for the results of his actions there is no repentance. Calvin calls it an indirect reprimand, reproving Adam for not perceiving his fault in his punishment: not simply that he was afraid at the voice of God, but that the voice of his judge was formidable to him because he was a sinner. The added clause about the command removes the pretext of ignorance.

Gill reads the answer as forced: not being able any longer to conceal the truth, though he shifts off the blame from himself. Henry finds the excuse frivolous. She gave him of the tree and pressed him to eat, which he did only to oblige her; but he ought to have taught her, not to have been taught by her, and it was no hard matter to determine which of the two he must be ruled by, his God or his wife. Worse, he words it so as tacitly to reflect on God himself — it is the woman whom thou gavest me, and gavest to be with me — insinuating that God was accessory, having given him the woman who gave him the fruit, so that he seemed to have it at but one remove from God's own hand. There is a strange proneness in those that are tempted to say they are tempted of God, as if our abusing God's gifts would excuse our violating God's laws. Clarke draws the practical conclusion. How few ingenuously confess their own sin: the subtlety of the tempter, the weakness of their own minds, the circumstances they were placed in, are pleaded; and till a man take his sin to himself and acknowledge that he alone is guilty, he cannot be humbled, and so cannot be saved.

Turning to the woman, Gill notes who she was — first in the transgression, and the one who drew her husband into it, upon whom he now seemingly casts the blame. Calvin says God contends no further with the man, since he aggravates rather than diminishes his crime, and though he rages he is yet held convicted. He would render the address more vehemently than the old interpreter: not why hast thou done this, but how hast thou done this, the language of one who wonders as at something prodigious — how was it possible that thou shouldst bring thy mind to be so perverse a counsellor to thy husband? Eve ought to have been confounded at the wickedness of which she was admonished; yet she is not struck dumb, but after the example of her husband transfers the charge, and by laying the blame on the serpent foolishly thinks herself absolved. Who compelled her to listen to his fallacies, and to place confidence in them more readily than in the word of God? Wesley sums the hearing up: neither of them owns the fault fully, and the prisoners being found guilty by their own confession, nothing material is offered in arrest of judgment.
14:
No question is put to the tempter, and the expositors ask why. Henry answers that God did not examine the serpent, nor ask him what he had done nor why he did it, but immediately sentenced him: because he was already convicted of rebellion, his malice openly avowed; and because he was to be for ever excluded from all hope of pardon. Why should anything be said to convince and humble him who was to find no place for repentance? His wound was not searched, because it was not to be cured. Gill says the same of the silence — no pains are taken to convince Satan of his sin, nor any time spent reasoning with him, he being a hardened apostate spirit without hope of mercy. Calvin turns the contrast toward us. God does not interrogate the serpent, since in the animal itself there was no sense of sin, and to the devil he would hold out no hope of pardon; he might by his own authority have sentenced Adam and Eve unheard. Why then call them to examination, except that he has a care for their salvation? There would be no need of any trial of the cause in order to condemn us; so while God insists upon extorting a confession, he acts rather as a physician than as a judge.

Clarke divides the sentence in two, one on Satan and the other on the agent he employed. The tempter is not asked why he deceived the woman, for he cannot roll the blame on any other: self-tempted he fell. The nachash, whom Clarke supposes to have stood at the head of the inferior animals and in a sort of intimacy with man, is to be greatly degraded, entirely banished from human society, and deprived of the gift of speech. Calvin finds the same doubleness in the wording — the language is of a mixed character, God so addressing the serpent that the last clause belongs to the devil. If it seem absurd that the punishment of another's fraud should be exacted from a brute animal, the solution is at hand: since it had been created for the benefit of man, there was nothing improper in its being accursed from the moment it was employed for his destruction. By this act of vengeance God would prove how highly he estimates the salvation of man, just as a father should hold in execration the sword by which his son had been slain. Henry puts the principle shortly: the devil's instruments must share in the devil's punishments, even the ox that killed a man being stoned.

On the curse itself Henry notes the reversal. Even the creeping things, when God made them, were blessed of him, but sin turned the blessing into a curse; the serpent that was more subtle than any beast of the field is here cursed above every beast of the field. His crime was that he tempted Eve to eat what she should not; his punishment was that he was necessitated to eat what he would not. Wesley reads the going and the eating as one figure: no longer upon feet, or half erect, but crawling along, the belly cleaving to the earth, and dust for food, which signifies a base and despicable condition. Calvin meets the objection that this is merely the serpent's nature. There is no absurdity in supposing that it was consigned again to the condition it was already naturally subject to, thrust back into its proper rank — thou, a wretched animal fixed to the earth, hast dared to rise up against man, and I now throw thee back to the place whence thou hast attempted to emerge. To eat dust is the sign of a vile and sordid nature, and Isaiah confirms it, promising under the reign of Christ that dust shall be the serpent's bread.
15:
Gill measures the enmity against the familiarity it replaced. Some conjecture that Eve had taken a particular liking to the creature and was delighted with it, laying it in her bosom or winding it about her neck for a bracelet, and that being a favourite it was chosen as the instrument to deceive her; but now she conceived an antipathy which has become natural between serpent and man, so that man abhors the sight of a serpent and the serpent the sight of man. It holds not of that serpent and that woman only, but of every serpent and every woman in successive ages, and of Satan and the church of God in all ages. Calvin reads the clause the same way at its first level: there should always be hostile strife between the human race and serpents, for by a secret feeling of nature man abhors them, and as often as the sight of one inspires us with horror the memory of our fall is renewed. Clarke will not have it. It is yet to be discovered that the serpentine race have any peculiar enmity against mankind; men have much more enmity to the common rat and the magpie, and serpents generally flee man's approach and avoid his dwelling.

The two nouns carry the weight. Calvin notes that there shall be such hatred that on both sides they are troublesome to each other, yet the Lord chastises man mercifully, not suffering Satan to touch him except in the heel, while he subjects the head of the serpent to be wounded; between head and heel there is a distinction of the superior and the inferior, and so God leaves some remains of dominion to man, that their condition should not be equal but man be superior in the conflict. From this he moves to the author of the mischief, since the Lord spoke not for the sake of the serpent but of the man — what end could it answer to thunder against a serpent in unintelligible words? Respect was had to men, both that they might dread sin the more, and that they might take consolation, perceiving that God is still propitious. Clarke arrives at the same place from the other end: it is evident that Satan, who actuated this creature, is alone intended in this part of the prophetic declaration, and God in his endless mercy has put enmity between men and him, so that though all mankind love his service, yet all invariably hate himself. Were it otherwise, who could be saved?

On the seed, Clarke presses the pronoun. It is He who shall bruise the head, and the person is to come by the woman, and by her alone, without the concurrence of man; therefore the address is not to Adam and Eve but to Eve only, and it was in consequence of this purpose of God that Jesus Christ was born of a virgin. He bruises the serpent's head in destroying his power over mankind, and Satan bruises his heel in that the salvation of man could only be brought about by the death of Christ — and the spiritual seed have the heel bruised often in persecution. Calvin corrects the Latin before expounding it: the feminine has crept in for the masculine, and on that corrupt reading a profane exposition has been built, applying to the mother of Christ what is said of her seed. He himself takes the seed as the posterity of the woman generally, and then, since not all the sons of Adam arise as conquerors, comes at last to one head in whom the victory lies. Wesley numbers what the promise gives notice of: Christ's incarnation, as the seed of the woman; his sufferings and death, pointed at in the bruising of the heel, that is, of his human nature; and his victory over Satan thereby.
16:
Gill notes the order: the woman receives her sentence next to the serpent and before the man, because she was first and more deeply in the transgression, and was the means of drawing her husband into it. Calvin notes the brevity. That the majesty of the judge may shine the more brightly, God uses no long disputation; and in bringing the serpent forward Eve thought she had herself escaped, and God, disregarding her cavils, condemns her. Let the sinner therefore, when he comes to the bar of God, cease to contend, lest he provoke the anger of him whom he has already too highly offended. Henry names the two heads under which the sentence falls — a state of sorrow and a state of subjection, proper punishments of a sin in which she had gratified her pleasure and her pride. Of the sorrow only one particular is specified, but it includes all those impressions of grief and fear which the mind of that tender sex is most apt to receive, and all the common calamities they are liable to. Sin brought sorrow into the world; had we known no guilt, we should have known no grief.

Clarke renders the doubled verb as multiplying I will multiply — I will multiply thy sorrows, and multiply those sorrows by other sorrows, during pregnancy and particularly in child-bearing. This curse has fallen in a heavier degree on the woman than on any other female; nothing is better attested, and yet there is certainly no natural reason why it should be so. It is a part of her punishment, and a part from which even God's mercy will not exempt her. Henry extends the multiplying in time: the sorrows include not only the travailing throes but the indispositions before, so that it is sorrow from the conception, and the nursing toils and vexations after; and if the children prove wicked and foolish they are more than ever the heaviness of her that bore them. Calvin thinks it credible that the woman would have brought forth without pain, or at least without such great suffering, had she stood in her original condition, and that her revolt from God subjected her to inconveniences of this kind. Wesley fixes on whose hand it is. It is God that multiplies our sorrows — I will do it — God as a righteous Judge, which ought to silence us, since as many as they are we have deserved them all and more; and God as a tender Father, for our necessary correction.

The second head is subjection. Henry says the whole sex, which by creation was equal with man, is for sin made inferior; the sentence amounts only to the apostolic command that wives be in subjection to their own husbands, but the entrance of sin has made that duty a punishment which otherwise it would not have been. Had man not sinned he would always have ruled with wisdom and love, and had the woman not sinned she would always have obeyed with humility and meekness, and then the dominion would have been no grievance: it is our own sin and folly that make our yoke heavy. Calvin puts it as a forcing back — she had previously been subject to her husband, but that was a liberal and gentle subjection, and now she is cast into servitude, the woman who had perversely exceeded her proper bounds being returned to her own position. Ellicott insists the woman is not cursed as the serpent was, but punished as next in guilt, and that her inferiority was tempered by a natural longing for the married state and by love. Among the heathen the punishment was made very bitter by the degradation to which woman was reduced; in Christ, as Paul teaches, the whole penalty has been abrogated.
17:
Gill notes that Adam comes last, being the last that sinned, but not therefore to be excused. Henry shows why the excuse fails: he laid the fault on his wife, but she could only tempt him, she could not force him, and though it was her fault to persuade him to eat, it was his fault to hearken to her. Men's frivolous pleas will in the day of God's judgment not only be overruled but turned against them, and made the grounds of their sentence — out of thine own mouth will I judge thee. Clarke puts the same charge in the second person: thou wast not deceived, she only gave and counselled thee to eat, and this thou shouldst have resisted. Keil and Delitzsch read the sentence as two punishments answering to two offences. First the cursing of the ground, then death, which affects the woman as well on account of their common guilt. By listening to his wife when she had been deceived, Adam had repudiated his superiority to the rest of creation, so that as a punishment nature would henceforth offer resistance to his will; and by breaking the divine command he had set himself above his Maker, so death would show him the worthlessness of his own nature.

Calvin defines the curse by its opposite. As the blessing of the earth means, in the language of Scripture, that fertility which God infuses by his secret power, so the curse is nothing else than the privation of it, when God withdraws his favour. Nor ought it to seem absurd that through the sin of man punishment should overflow the innocent earth; for as the outermost sphere was thought to carry all the heavens round with it, so the ruin of man drives headlong all those creatures which were formed for his sake. Before the fall the state of the world was a most fair and delightful mirror of the divine favour; now, in all the elements, we perceive that we are cursed — though the Lord still sprinkles everywhere the tokens of his goodness, so that David may truly say the earth is full of his mercy. Wesley puts the change in a sentence: the earth by the sin of man is made subject to vanity, its several parts not so serviceable to man's comfort as they were when they were made. Henry marks the mercy in the wording. Adam himself is not cursed, as the serpent was, but only the ground for his sake; he is yet above ground, and the earth continues to be his habitation.

Of the thorns and thistles Gill says they were given not for his advantage but to give him more trouble, and to cause him more fatigue and sorrow to root them up; they include all sorts of noxious herbs and troublesome weeds, added to man's labour so that those more useful might grow and flourish. Rabbi Eliezer was of opinion that had there been no new blessing upon the earth it would have brought forth nothing else. Clarke thinks much more is implied than generally appears, and demonstrates it by counting. The amazing fertility of the commonest thistles makes them the proper instruments for fulfilling this sentence: one species bears about eighty heads, each holding some three hundred seeds, and the fourth year's growth from a single plant would be more than enough to stock the surface of every planet in the solar system. Calvin draws the conclusion the count implies. Whatsoever unwholesome things may be produced are not natural fruits of the earth, but corruptions which originate from sin; and it is not our part to expostulate with the earth as if it were maliciously frustrating our purpose, but in its sterility to mark the anger of God, and mourn over our own sins.
19:
Gill reads the sweat of the face literally and then widely. The Hebrew is of thy nose, sweat appearing first on the forehead and trickling down by the nose in men at hard labour; and it takes in all the operations by which the earth is made to yield bread — ploughing, sowing, reaping, threshing, winnowing, grinding, sifting, kneading, baking. It reaches further still, for even those exercises which depend upon the brain are not excused from the expense, so that no man in any station of life is exempt from the sentence, and none until he dies. Clarke explains the physiology, and turns it into a memorial. The forehead is the first part whence the sweat issues, because the blood is strongly propelled to the head, partly by stooping but chiefly by the action of the muscles, so that the vessels become turgid, the fibres relax, the pores enlarge, and the serum is poured out. The very commencement of every man's labour may thus put him in mind of his sin and its consequences. Wesley marks only the change: his business before he sinned was a constant pleasure to him, and now his labour shall be a weariness.

Calvin is at pains to say what the verse is not. Under cover of this passage certain ignorant persons would rashly impel all men to manual labour, but God is not here teaching as a master or legislator; he is denouncing punishment as a judge. Had a rule been prescribed, it would be necessary for all to become husbandmen, no place would be given to the mechanical arts, and we must go out of the world to seek clothing and the other necessaries of life. What God pronounces from his judgment-seat is that the life of man shall henceforth be miserable, because Adam had proved himself unworthy of that tranquil and joyful state for which he was created. Should any object that many are inactive and indolent, that does not prevent the curse from having spread over the whole race: some flee from troubles and more do all they can to grasp at immunity from them, but the Lord subjects all without exception to this yoke. Labour is nevertheless not imposed equally on each, and God often remits a portion of the curse to his own children, lest they sink beneath the burden — some will rise early and go late to rest and eat the bread of carefulness, but the Lord gives his beloved sleep.

On the return to dust, Ellicott argues that mortality was the body's own condition. A spiritual being is eternal by its own constitution, and the argument by which Butler proves the soul immortal equally proves the body mortal, since death is the division of a compound substance into its parts and the soul is simple and incapable of division. The body of Adam, composed of particles of earth, was capable of division, and our first parents were assured of unending existence by a special gift typified in the tree of life; that gift being now withdrawn, the sweat of man's brow was itself proof that he was returning to his earth, for it told of exhaustion and waste. Clarke draws the same inference from the sentence: man would have been immortal had he never transgressed, and that state of continual life and health depended on his obedience, the tree of life being the appointed means of continual preservation. Calvin adds that the dying had already begun, this accursed life being nothing else than the beginning of death. When Adam was raised so high that the glory of the divine image shone in him, the terrestrial origin of his body was almost obliterated; despoiled of that excellence, what remains but that by his departure out of life he should recognise himself to be earth?
20:
Clarke complains that a reader without the original cannot see the reason given: what has the word Eve to do with being the mother of all living? The Septuagint is literal and correct in rendering the name Life, for the Hebrew Chavvah, which we have corrupted into Eve, a word destitute of all meaning, answers exactly to the Greek. Gill agrees on the root: the name comes not from the verb to show forth or declare, as though she were so called for being talkative — the guess of some Jewish writers — but from the verb to live, as the reason given in the text shows. He adds that the word survives in heathen writers, being repeated in the Bacchanalian rites where the worshippers appeared with serpents platted on their heads, so that Bacchus is sometimes called Evius. Henry sets the two names side by side. God named the man and called him Adam, which signifies red earth; Adam, in further token of dominion, named the woman and called her Eve, that is, life. Adam bears the name of the dying body, Eve that of the living soul; he had called her woman before, as a wife, and here calls her life, as a mother.

What the naming meant divides them. Henry offers two readings: if it was done by divine direction it was an instance of God's favour, and, like the new naming of Abraham and Sarah, a seal of the covenant and an assurance that the blessing to be fruitful and multiply had not been reversed; if Adam did it of himself it was an instance of his faith in the word of God, not in contempt or defiance of the curse, but in humble confidence and dependence upon the blessing. Calvin weighs whether Moses meant rather to tax Adam with thoughtlessness, who, being himself immersed in death, yet gave his wife so proud a name; he concludes that as soon as Adam had escaped present death, being encouraged by a measure of consolation, he celebrated that divine benefit in the name — though it does not follow that he triumphed over death as he ought. Keil and Delitzsch have no such hesitation: it was through the power of divine grace that Adam believed the promise concerning the woman's seed, and manifested his faith in the name he gave his wife. Ellicott adds the tenderness. Through her alone could human life be continued, and Adam, having no word of reproach for her, turns from his own punishment to call her his compensation for his loss.

The clothing is read as both a mercy and a warning. Calvin cautions against taking the words as if God had been a furrier, or a servant to sew clothes; the skins did not come by chance: the pair, impelled by a new necessity, put animals to death and covered themselves, having been divinely directed to that counsel, and so Moses calls God its author. Why skins? Because garments of that material would look more degrading than linen or woollen, so that in such a dress they should behold their own vileness, as they had before seen it in their nakedness — an example, too, of a frugal and inexpensive mode of dress. Wesley finds a further significancy: the beasts whose skins they were must be slain, slain before their eyes, to show them what death is, and probably slain for sacrifice, to typify the great sacrifice which in the latter end of the world should be offered once for all; so the first thing that died was Christ in a figure. Henry sets the two coverings against each other. The aprons of fig-leaves were a covering too narrow to wrap themselves in, and such are all the rags of our own righteousness; but the coats of skin were large and strong and durable and fit for them.
22:
Henry hears the sentence as an upbraiding, and reads the tone into it: a goodly god he makes, does he not — see what he has got, what preferments, what advantages, by eating forbidden fruit. It was said to awaken and humble them, that, seeing themselves deceived by following the devil's counsel, they might pursue the happiness God should offer in the way he should prescribe. God thus fills their faces with shame, that they may seek his name, and puts them to this confusion in order to their conversion. Wesley keeps the reproof and drops the sarcasm. Calvin keeps both: an ironical reproof, by which God would not only prick the heart of man but pierce it through and through — though he does not cruelly triumph over the miserable and afflicted, but, according to the necessity of the disease, applies a more violent remedy. And it was a sad and horrid spectacle: that he in whom the glory of the divine image had lately shone should lie hidden under fetid skins to cover his own disgrace, and that there should be more comeliness in a dead animal than in a living man.

Three others refuse the irony outright. Clarke says the difficulty is increased by our translation, since the Hebrew verb is preterite — was, not is — as it stands also in the Samaritan, the Syriac and the Septuagint; which points to an ellipsis, and yields the paraphrase that the man who was like one of us in purity and wisdom is now fallen and robbed of his excellence, having added to the knowledge of the good, by his transgression, the knowledge of the evil. Some suppose the words spoken ironically, by a cutting taunt; but God is ever consistent with himself, and his infinite pity prohibited the use of either sarcasm or irony in speaking of so dreadful a catastrophe. Keil and Delitzsch put it more sharply still: irony at the expense of a wretched tempted soul might well befit Satan, but not the Lord, and the likeness is predicated only with regard to the knowledge of good and evil, in which the man really had become like God. Ellicott finds the same thing painful and humiliating in Chrysostom and the other Fathers who took it so. By the fall man had sunk morally but grown mentally: he had asserted his independence and attained a knowledge without which his endowment of free-will would have remained in abeyance.

Why the tree of life is barred, Ellicott answers from mercy: if an unending physical life were added to the gift of free-will now in revolt against God, the condition of man would become most miserable. He is still to attain immortality, but now through struggle, sorrow, penitence, faith and death; hence a paradise is no fit home for him. Henry finds a warning in it. There is a foolish proneness in those who have made themselves unworthy of the substance of Christian privileges to catch at the signs and shadows of them, and it is not only justice but kindness to deny them. Yet he marks how far the sentence stops short: Adam was sent to a place of toil, not to a place of torment, to the ground and not to the grave, to hold the plough and not to drag the chain. Gill says he was put away as a man puts away his wife when he divorces her, or as a prince banishes a rebellious subject, and yet was not sent to hell at once, as the apostate angels were. Calvin gathers the mitigations: banished from the palace of which he had been lord, he obtained elsewhere a place to dwell; bereft of his delicacies, he was still supplied with food; excommunicated from the tree of life, he was offered a new remedy in sacrifices.
24:
Gill takes the verb from the law of divorce. Being unwilling to go out upon the orders given, some degree of force was used; and the word by which it is expressed is used of divorces. There was a conjugal relation between God and man, the covenant between them having the nature of a matrimonial contract, which man broke by believing the devil rather than his husband; wherefore God wrote him a bill of divorce and sent him away, driving him from his presence and communion, from his seat of pleasure and garden of delight — an emblem of that separation and distance which sin makes between God and his creature. Clarke notes three things in the one clause: God's displeasure against sinful man, evidenced by expelling him from this place of blessedness; man's unfitness for the place, of which he had rendered himself unworthy; and his reluctance to leave it, for he was unwilling to depart, and God drove him out. Ellicott agrees that the verb implies displeasure and compulsion, and that Adam went with the consciousness that he had incurred the divine anger. Wesley reads the expulsion as the exclusion of him and his guilty race from that communion with God which was the bliss and glory of paradise.

What the guards were, the two commentators who ask cannot agree. Clarke first corrects the English: Hebrew masculine plurals end in im, and to add an s when the word is brought over is improper, so it should be written cherubim. As to what they were, he says they are utterly unknown and the conjectures endless. From the tabernacle and temple descriptions they appear sometimes with two faces, those of a lion and of a man, while in Ezekiel they have four faces and four wings — a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle — with but one body to these heads. Since the word never appears as a verb, he takes it to be compounded of a particle of resemblance and a root meaning to be great or powerful, and so reads the cherubim as emblematical representations of the eternal power and Godhead. Ellicott takes the ordinary derivation instead, from a root signifying to carve or grave, and especially to plough, which with the description of the mercy-seat suggests that the cherubim were winged bulls, probably with human heads, like those brought from Nineveh. He expressly warns against confounding them with the four living creatures of Ezekiel's vision, which are the beasts of the Revelation and have a far different office and signification.

Their office is not in dispute. Ellicott says the cherub is here to guard the garden lest man should try to force an entrance back, as the cherubs upon the mercy-seat were to protect it from impious approach. Wesley describes a detachment armed with a dreadful and irresistible power, represented by flaming swords which turned every way, posted on that side of the garden which lay next to the place whither Adam was sent, to keep the way that led to the tree of life. Clarke understands by the sword turning every way, or the flame folding back upon itself, the formidable appearances these beings assumed to render the passage inaccessible; and he thinks they were so employed only for a time, since it is probable that God soon removed the tree of life and abolished the garden, so that its situation could never afterwards be positively ascertained. He closes the chapter as a tragedy in which all the actors are slain: the serpent degraded, the woman cursed with pains and subjection, the man doomed to incessant toil, the earth cursed with barrenness, the garden interdicted. Yet in the midst of wrath God remembers mercy, and a promise of redemption from this cursed state is made through him who in the fullness of time is to be made flesh.
